utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-87-T, the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome back to the courtroom to continue our consideration of the various challenging issues raised by this trial. We will now proceed -- continue to hear the Defence case for the fifth accused, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, thank you for your welcome. First of all, I would like to wish everyone a happy new year and for our work in 2008 to be at least as successful as it was in 2007. Our next witness is Goran Jevtovic, a colonel of Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jevtovic. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of the accused, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jevtovic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please be so kind and tell us your full name for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the 24th of December of 2007 did you make a written statement to General Lazarevic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to go through that statement to check what it says and did you eventually sign it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a chance to read it carefully and to reassure myself everything was accurate. I eventually signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If you were to be asked the same questions on the same subject matter today would you still provide the same answers as you did for the purposes of that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would provide the same answers, those that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, in order to speed things up a little, which was after all the purpose of the statement that you made, there is no need for us to rehash what you stated in your statement. I will merely ask you a couple of additional questions and perhaps show you a number of exhibits. I would like to move on immediately to 5D1172.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do, the statement is 5D1385; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. I apologise for omitting to point that out for the benefit of the Chamber. I also move that it be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we briefly have the statement on the screen. I'm particularly concerned about the English, and I would like to see paragraph 8 of the English. Now, if you look at this you'll see that some of the letters in the translation are not letters but just simply marks like dashes or brackets or whatever and it's to do with the formatting. Now, it doesn't matter for today, Mr. Bakrac, but I think this should be replaced by a version which is clearly all language and not punctuation in parts where letters should be. It's to do with electronic formulation and you can do it at your convenience. It can be read as it is, but it's more -- it ought to be done in proper form at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. I do apologise, but this is an official translation from CLSS. I asked the CLSS to translate these statements for us on purpose. I thought there was a typing error on our part, at least in our hard copy. I will do my best to set things right. I will also draw the attention of CLSS to these errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please see what you can do, but as I say it's not vital, we can read it as it stands, but it's something to try to avoid in case it is repeated -- certainly repeated in other later statements. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Exhibit 5D1172.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I do. In the second half July, as the document reflects, it was received among others by the forward command post of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, in paragraphs 16, 17, and 18 of your statement you made comments concerning Prosecution Exhibit P969 which is a command [as interpreted] of the Pristina Corps command about Djakovica signed by the Chief of Staff, the then-Colonel Lazarevic. The order is about not firing on terrorists if there were foreign and international representatives of the peace mission in the area. Was this something that was based on a Pristina Corps document, specifically item 1 of this order dated the 7th of July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent that I can remember that seems to be correct. It has been a long time, however. All the other documents and orders that were drafted based on this one were produced early in July, bearing in mind that the date on the one you're talking about is the 7th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we now please have 5D1174.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the paragraphs that I'm referring to, 16, 17, and 18, contain a detailed explanation of what documents such as the one we've just looked at are about. There is no need to dwell on this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, you have in front of you 5D1174.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 2 of this document, item 3, the situation in the army's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please comment on the first paragraph of that item, or rather, in order to speed things up a little you said in your statement something about the Glodjane, Rznic, and Prilep actions and also something about the Slup and Voksa actions. You commented about those orders as well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question is this: At the time these actions were carried out, did the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, Mr. Perisic, along with the team from his General Staff spend some time in the Djakovica area, which was where these actions took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's a well-known activity that was carried out by the General Staff. It was a specific mission for this General Staff team that arrived in the area to inspect and check the situation across the corps' units and the 3rd Army. The team was led by the Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, in person. There was a team comprising a number of people, generals and colonels. There were documents and a plan that this inspection was based on. This all happened at this very time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can one actually see that based on this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is an operations report of the 3rd Army command. It's a report that was produced at the forward command post of the 3rd Army, and all I have in front of me now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Item 3, it's implicit if we look at item 3, it is crystal clear. In paragraph 1 whoever produced this report emphasises that checks were continued and units of the Yugoslav Army in Kosovo and Metohija were still being inspected. I won't read any further, but this tallies with what I've been saying. It even says that the team was to return on the 15th of August at 0800 hours. I do remember that very clearly since I was the operative organ at this forward command post, and I know what the plan was that had arrived. This activity was based in its entirety on a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. My next question is: What about the Chief of the General Staff, Mr. Perisic, was he familiar with these actions that you have been talking about and you have been commenting on documents in relation to these actions: Glodjane, Slup, and Voksa, was he familiar with all the details of these actions, and did he make any remarks about these actions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A question phrased in that way has no foundation. There is no foundation for this witness to comment on General Perisic's awareness and what he was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we establish a foundation, Mr. Bakrac? In other words, what's the source of the witness's knowledge about Perisic's state of knowledge. Could you ask him that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understood him to be saying in the B/C/S that he knew this very well because he was there when the inspection took place. Maybe it was a case of poor interpretation, but I can ask him again. I'm just trying to speed this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, were you present for the briefing to the Chief of the General Staff about these actions and who did the briefing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present there. He was briefed on these actions. This was part of a general briefing. He was the Chief of the General Staff after all, and I was present there because I was an operative officer at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica. I remember really well his arrival and the arrival of his team as well as the briefing itself or, for that matter, in general their entire stay in the Pristina Corps in the state border area specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who did the briefing for the benefit of the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Pristina Corps at the time, General Pavkovic, in the presence of all the other organs from the Pristina Corps command who were at the time at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I asked you a question but the we didn't have time to hear your answer because my learned friend had an objection to raise. What about the Chief of the General Staff, Mr. Perisic, did he raise any objections? Did he make any comments regarding this briefing, the briefing about these actions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Quite the contrary, in fact. He was quite satisfied at least as far as the official part of the briefing was concerned, which is the part that I attended, and I can state this for the record. There were reports about this that they produced as a team and those reports were very upbeat. Their entire stay, the entire inspection ran smoothly and in a very positive tone. There were briefings, there were reports that were submitted, certain proposals were adopted, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Let us look at item 5 on this document very briefly just a single sentence that I am interested in. The second paragraph of that item, it's a single sentence really and tell me if this decision of the 3rd Army command reflects what you saw in the Slup and Voksa orders signed by the Chief of Staff General Lazarevic which you explained in detail. Is that consistent with the action the decision being taken here by the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely item 5 in its entirety and particularly the second paragraph of item 5 talks about the fact that the army commander was behind the involvement of this Combat Group of the 15th Armoured Brigade, number 3 which was to lend support to MUP forces and so on and so forth, whatever the paragraph goes on to state. This was the established practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, let us now look at 6D692. Colonel, it appears to be on the screen and do you recognise this document and can you very briefly comment on it, please?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The title of this document that was developed at the command of the Pristina Corps in Pristina is a preparatory order for support to MUP forces, and the commander of the corps practically from his -- based on his own competences and estimates made on the ground and all these circumstances practically informs the units or maybe gives them some initial preparatory, preliminary, tasks for the purposes of their general preparation for something that will follow from a further decision or some other document. This is indeed enumerated item by item, combat group by combat group, covering all the forces that would be eligible to participate. So this is a preparatory order for units that may be involved pursuant to some future document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And after that the actions we discussed followed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, before we move on, I believe it's a misinterpretation, could you -- or a mistranslation. Could you read the title of the document. It says: "Addressed to the commander personally," I think it's a mistranslation in English. Can you read it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: "Preparatory order to support or for support to MUP forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is now corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an official military term, Envisaged by military legislation and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the next document, 5D206.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We see the title: "Command group PrK, 30th March 1999." Could you explain briefly what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move to page 2 where we see initials G.J..

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you prepare this document? Could you comment briefly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It's a regular combat report, and I indeed prepared this document. I developed it, and I actually made it on the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So on the 30th of March there was no forward command post, there was just the combat group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Command group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was a command group which is of a smaller strength than a forward command post, and the purpose of that command group was explained in my statement. As such, it was based close to the border in the area of Metohija and its purposes and its tasks were mainly to link up our forces, forces of the Pristina Corps, and units that were reinforcing the Pristina Corps in defending the state border against the aggression that had, by that time, begun. And of course that command group had the obligation to produce regular and as-required interim combat reports as well as all and any other documents envisaged by rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If we look at item 7, it appears -- and we will see something about it later in a further document. It appears that almost every day on the border there were clashes with terrorists from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This report is representative, as we see in item 7, because on the previous day, the 29th of March on the axis indicated here, which is the broader area of Babaj Boks village, a large group of terrorists was intercepted carrying quite a large amount of equipment and weapons. And it was a serious event, a serious incident on the border. It was practically an incursion and an attack on security forces because at that time the forces that were to be deployed in securing the state border had not been deployed yet and had not taken up positions envisaged. So it was a classic attack that they mounted. It is one of the most serious incidents as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I would now like to move on to the next document, Exhibit 5D210. To move on more quickly while we're waiting, it's another combat report of the command group of the Pristina Corps dated 9 April. It's still named "command group." Could you comment on this document because I believe on page 2 we will again find initially G.J., you seem to be the author.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I am the author, and I am particularly proud of it because that day was practically the beginning of an open attack from the Republic of Albania across a wide front. I did this report to describe the situation as of 11.00 a.m. That's the moment, that's the day when the land aggression by Siptar terrorist forces began with a main attack on Karaula-Kosare axis. Losses were incurred, our forces were relatively weak, and the situation on that day is reflected by my penultimate sentence which reads: "Combat morale is at a high level," which was true, "and we shall defend the border at any cost." Such language is rarely used in military terminology, but that sentence reflects the fierceness of that attack across a wide front, as I said. And item 6 is also telling because before the beginning of the ground aggression an organized disruption of all types of communication was executed so that militarily speaking the forces in the first military echelon, those on the state border, were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, let me interrupt you. I have a few subquestions. Was the Kosare border post defended? Did the enemy penetrate in-depth of our territory and how long did this ground attack on Kosare border post last, that is, the attack between the Kosare border post and Morina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The attack on that axis Kosare-Morina and further on across other border posts lasted without cessation with the same intensity. On the 9th of April we managed to fend off the enemy which was very, very large in numbers on the very line of the state border, but things started to get complicated a day or two later when the border post fell, the very structure of the border post, and two dominating elevations, Rasa Kosare and Maja Glava features. What is important and what I wish to say is that from that day on the intensity of the attack from Albania by enormous, I would say, forces of the terrorists who were well led increased and built up --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Colonel, but our time is limited. Tell me, how long was that attack? My second me was: Did they penetrate behind the lines inside the territory of the Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did penetrate, not perhaps at the first moment, but the next day. They penetrated indeed on the first day, engaged in combat, and the next day they had practically taken control of the border post and they were already 500 metres deep into the territory on two sub-axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How long was the attack?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It started at 4.00 a.m. on the 9th of April with strong artillery preparation, and it did not stop until the end of the war. So until the end of the war 24 hours a day it went on with extremely strong air support and artillery support from the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said here that there was no telephone communication or any other communication with the corps command. Did anyone from the corps command on the 9th or the 10th of April come to this location, to this axis of attack?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Not on the 9th of April. On the 9th of April I just sent my report, Colonel Drajkovic was wounded as you can see in my report on the first page, but on the 10th of April sometime around noon if I remember correctly, after receiving this report, the corps commander, General Lazarevic, arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go any further, do I rightly understand that throughout the time of this attack, which was from the 9th of April until the end of the war, the degree or the extent of penetration into your territory was only 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that's what I said about those two sub-axes, 500 metres is a large area, it's a long distance when we are speaking about penetration into the sovereign territory of a state, that they were keeping, they were holding those 500 metres. But incursions from the terrorist forces from Albania went even deeper. However, not in the same numbers as in that part of the front line which I described on those two axes or sub-axes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, you said that the corps commander inspected those locations on the 10th of April. All that time until the end of the war you were at the forward command post in Djakovica, that command post changed throughout the war. After the 10th of April did the corps commander come again to Djakovica at any time; and if so, when was his next visit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this very well because I was there all the time in Djakovica, not only in Djakovica but in that broader area. And if I can remember correctly after all this time, sometime in the second half of May or in the end of May in 1999, I and all of us at the forward command post saw General Lazarevic for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. Let us look at 5D230, that's -- we see it's no longer the command group of the Pristina Corps, it's the command of the Pristina Corps forward command post combat report. Let us look at page 2. It's dated 26 May 1999. Is that the right date? You said in your statement that after that ground aggression General Lazarevic came again to Djakovica only once more in the second half of May. Here we see a combat report from the 26th of May, item 2. Could you read just one sentence, it's short, is that it? Is that what you meant when you said in your statement that he came once again in the second half of May?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. In the first paragraph it is written that in the area of responsibility of the forward command post the commander of the 3rd Army and the commander of the Pristina Corps paid a visit. I made this report personally. It was signed by the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, Colonel Velimir Zivkovic, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, you spoke to us about the breakthrough across the state border and the permanent aggression on the axis Kosare border post Morina, the penetration into our territory by Albanian terrorists, and you said that it lasted until the end of the war. Can you tell us about that axis? Where does it end inside the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and what is that region called?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: That axis is part of a broader axis, but I would denominate as Kosare- Liken border post, and now this sub-axis, Kosare-Morina, leads towards Djakovica, that is, Radonjic Lake, passing through river-beds, river valleys. On our topographic maps we see that it goes through river valleys. It's an axis of some operative significance. It is passable for tanks, and in the course of the war it turned out that the axis was important in terms of admitting staged landing by forces, enemy forces, into Kosovo and Metohija. And that's why activity and aggression along that axis went on very intensively until the last day of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "river valleys," does that valley of a river also have a different name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I know the local population called it "Caragoj valley." In fact, it's not about valley. On the official topographic map of Yugoslavia it's not just a river, it's an area that stretches from Junik village until Djakovica, and it's crisscrossed area in the sense of manoeuvres. It is not a typical valley. It is -- it's a large wooded area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any intelligence or any other sort of information indicating that in the Caragoj valley there was a KLA brigade that was active?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, given the time that has passed - and I remember quite well even though I ceased dealing with intelligence and counter-intelligence affairs - there was information indicating that terrorists were active there, quite strong forces the size of a brigade, equivalent to a brigade. We received daily information about their activities. First of all, during that long period of time they attacked especially MUP check-points as well as columns and individual vehicles of the army and Pristina Corps moving about in that area in the Caragoj valley which is the border area of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that on the 27th and 28th of April in the territory of the Reka valley there was an action carried out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that. The term "action" was a jargon term, and I stress this quite knowledgeably. Why do I do so? Because this so-called action -- no document was prepared for this so-called action, and these events came about precisely as a result of something that I have spoken of earlier, namely, continuous activity of Siptar terrorists and this brigade of theirs which incessantly put at risk the combat disposition of the units in the first combat echelon and it also put at risk communication, or rather, roads, Decani-Djakovica and Prizren as well as other roads leading to our border post, to our border, which were of major importance for us. So this action came as a result of what I have spoken of earlier. We are dealing now with the sweeping of the terrain. This was an attempt to suppress Siptar terrorist forces in this broader area and to render them harmless to the combat disposition of the units, not just units but all other forces there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly who participated and how in this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was, combat action and the search and sweeping of the terrain that was conducted in that valley was something that the MUP forces were tasked with. As far as I remember, PJP units were tasked with this. As for the units of the Pristina Corps, their role was to, in coordination with the MUP, to safeguard our combat disposition and the road between Decani and Djakovica as well as the perimeter of the town of Djakovica, the outlying areas of Djakovica. Before the action began, if I remember correctly, I think that three companies of PJP units were to participate; however, for some reason one of the companies could not be engaged. I think that it was the company from Pec or perhaps that's how they referred to it. I'm not sure of its precise name right now. And then the problem of the insufficient number of members of MUP emerged. However, I'd like to stress that our combat disposition first and foremost our battalion in the first combat echelon was at risk on a daily basis. I do not want to repeat what I have already stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you can clarify something for me. The action that you're talking about is the action in coordination with the MUP to safeguard your combat disposition and the road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there was no order or decision in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no written decision or order as basic documents were produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is a situation where you had tasks but no order. So how did you know your tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, those were the tasks that stemmed or originated from regular duties, routine duties, of units in the area. If I were to try to explain this in a bit more graphic terms, this is how I would put it. We have a combat disposition of a unit which is located in a certain sector, and this combat disposition is intended for the defence of the state border which is constantly at risk due to terrorist activity over a prolonged period of time. So in a way, that was an ongoing duty of those who were out in the field. To put it in other terms, if somebody attacks you, you have to protect yourself given something that was confirmed later, namely, that those were quite strong terrorist forces that were located in several villages in the Caragoj valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, perhaps we could assist everyone to understand this by looking at Exhibit P2019, which is the combat log of the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade, and the date is the 26th of April, 1999. This page is marked Y0045827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be, Mr. Bakrac, that this document is under seal. Can you assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, Your Honour. Perhaps the Prosecutor could help us, but I don't think so. P2019 no, I'm being told that it is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case, please ensure that it's not exhibited out with the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, could we move into private session, please, so that we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you going to be reading parts of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one sentence on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall move into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you ask anything else, to be very clear about this, Mr. Jevtovic, are you saying that that records an order for the action that was carried out on the 27th and 28th of April or do you still say that what happened on the 27th and 28th of April was simply spontaneous response to routine activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I didn't say that it was a spontaneous response to routine activity. I didn't use those terms. All I said was that no document was produced in the form of an order. As for combat disposition, combat disposition of every unit needs to be defended, given that this activity in the Caragoj valley was carried out, part of the forces of the army, that is to say of the Pristina Corps, was engaged in a broader area to block off a sector that that unit held in accordance with the plan on the defence activities which had been prepared much earlier. In this particular case, the Chief of Staff conveyed tasks orally to the commander of the unit, and these tasks pertained to what I have mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I remain confused, I'm afraid. You did tell us that your tasks originated from regular duties, routine duties. Are you now telling us these tasks were actually instructed by General Zivkovic or perhaps he was colonel at the time? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, he was colonel at the time. The tasks that he gave practically represented putting into action something that was duty of the units to begin with, and the tasks that he conveyed to the commander of the unit were, in fact, something that came as a result of the coordination with the MUP organs aimed at suppressing the activities of that terrorist brigade which was located in that area. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we've seen doesn't refer to coordination, though, so where did that emerge from, that you were to coordinate with certain MUP units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the document that I see now in front of me in e-court is the document which was produced at a lower command level, in a tactical unit, something that's called a tactical unit. Commander of a unit is not duty-bound to be informed of all of the results of coordination or planning of a particular action. In order to be even clearer, let me say this: He was given the tasks that concerned him, his unit, and the sector where they were located. Further on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful. No doubt someone will then show us later any document that might assist in identifying where the coordination was arranged, or it may even be that we have already in process a document which clarifies that. So we needn't trouble you further on that, Mr. Jevtovic. Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, do you know Captain Nike Peraj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Nike Peraj. Yes, I know him really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when this witness testified in private session, and there was also another witness who testified in private session, so therefore may we please move briefly into private session so that we can ascertain how this witness came to know Peraj and since when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that appropriate, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where was the HQ of the forward command post on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of April in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the HQ of the forward command post of the Pristina Corps was in the centre of town. It was housed in a building of a construction company in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where were the offices of this forward command post?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Their offices, or rather, this building was actually located between two residential buildings. It was a three-storey building. There was a ground floor and a basement in which the files of this company were kept. This was the centre of town. It was near the main department store near the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Nike Peraj ever go to the forward command post, and especially did he go there on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, never, never. He never went there nor could he have, given his duty at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness Peraj in his statement and before this Court stated that on the 28th of April in the morning hours at about 9.00, to be more specific, he arrived at the command, the forward command post, where he found you and General Lazarevic in the basement of that building in your and Lazarevic's office running the Reka operation and marking all of this on a map. Is that statement truthful?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is not just a lie, it's a blatant lie. It's a blatant fabrication and is entirely baseless. I can go on explaining for as long as you like me to but the truth of the matter is --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's just try to speed this long, if possible. Was General Lazarevic in Djakovica on those days that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, certainly not. As I said a while ago, he certainly wasn't in that basement to begin with. He never set foot there in that basement. I don't think he even knows that there was a basement in that building to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's try to cut this short. My question, we have an assumption, let's talk about this assumption, the assumption being General Lazarevic as commander of the Pristina Corps was there where Nike Peraj claims to have found him. Could Nike Peraj just have walked into that building, walked into that basement, walked into that office, stand right there next to you unmonitored and watch you discuss something and make markings on a map?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: That is sheer nonsense. A forward command post, as the name implies, is a command post. It is secured in keeping with particular procedures. A command post is a place of command. There is an outer perimeter of security, if you like; there is a system of internal security in place; there is reception; and this is an organized place with security measures, especially at a time of war. These are paramount, the security measures. When a commander arrives at a command post, the situation is quite particular because each commander under wartime conditions has his own security that follows him around. We have a security system, we have reception in place, there would have been additional forces, especially if General Lazarevic as the corps commander had been there; and this doesn't just apply to Nike Peraj, it applies to everyone else such as the brigade commanders, for example. They weren't just free to walk into that command post unannounced. I think the only person who actually had approval to access the building was the garrison commander at the time, General Djose [phoen]. Those occupying the external security perimeter and those at reception would normally get in touch with me since I was the operative officer there, whoever on duty, and then I would go there or maybe an officer would send somebody else there, whichever officer was in charge, and they would see this person and most of these conversations ended right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say when they went there to see these people and most of the conversations ended right there. Right where? Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Outside this building, the agency for construction land. Maybe you want me to draw up the ground plan so you see what it's like. There's an entrance, there's a small internal hall and there's a small corridor inside the building and there's a stair case leading up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So it was inside that hall that it ended for the most part?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was outside this hall because that meant the person would have already accessed the forward command post; but we didn't receive anyone, we didn't receive any parties. This would have been too much for us to deal with at the time since there was so many things happening along the border. We didn't even have enough time to share a cup of coffee undisturbed let alone to receive parties for anyone to go there for the purposes of just simply obtaining information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In paragraph 29, 30, and 31 of your statement, Colonel, because I do have to wrap this up now, you provided detailed account in relation to all the other statements that Nike Peraj made. It's all written down there and the Chamber can see for themselves. I thank you for your evidence, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jevtovic, on the 27th and 28th of April were you in the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I rule, I would be there in the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just tell me whether you were there on the 27th and 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not during the day. Every morning I would go to the border area, most often to Morina or Kosare border posts, and the same applies to those two days, at least as far as I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know where Peraj was on the 27th and 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't, I really don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see him on those two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know where General Lazarevic was on the 27th and 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. I don't know where General Lazarevic was on the 27th and 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does any Defence counsel -- Mr. -- Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, good afternoon, sir. I'm Dan Ivetic, one of the attorneys for Sreten Lukic, and this afternoon I will have some questions for you. Please pay close attention to the questions and try to give me concise answers. Now, first of all, looking at your statement this 5D1385, and specifically focusing your attention on paragraph 11 of the statement in both the B/C/S and the English, in English it's page 4, in B/C/S I believe it's page -- I believe it's page -- it is also page 4 on the B/C/S as well. In any event, you mentioned that all MUP requests for support had to be collected through the MUP staff for KiM. You were never an eye-witness to any such requests actually originating from the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija, are you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I believe I don't understand your question. I was never an eye-witness to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You never witnessed any such request originating from the MUP staff in KiM? That is to say you never saw any such request from the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija, did you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No written requests in the form of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While we're on this, could you, Mr. Jevtovic, could you read the first sentence of paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I remember well that the 3rd Army commander, General Samardzic, had already ordered that all MUP requests for support had to be collected through the MUP staff for KiM and that the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. That's all. The word "collected" in English didn't sound right, but apparently that's the word. Please continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, you said: "No written requests in the form of a document," at page 30, line 9. Am I correct that you never witnessed any such requests coming from the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija in any other form as well? You were never a witness to anything like that, were you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I did not -- a MUP document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, and my question is: You did not witness any other type of request apart from -- even -- you did not witness any oral requests coming from the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija for their support either, did you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I did witness oral requests. Oral requests are one thing. Written documents are a different thing altogether. I don't remember ever seeing a written document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What did you receive from the staff of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - this having been quite a long time ago - at the Djakovica forward command post we received nothing from the MUP staff, not even the information or anything like that to the extent that we were concerned in the Metohija area, everything came through the Pristina Corps command and the commander, of course, and also through our documents. Sometimes we exchanged information, there was some coordination linking up that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to clear up or move to another area of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you understand any of that, Mr. Ivetic? If you're happy, then please carry on, but it's incomprehensible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try then to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, are you aware personally of any request for support coming from the MUP? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, from the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not from the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's simple, isn't it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, how do you say that you witnessed some of the oral requests? What do you mean by that? I'm also confused. What do you mean by stating that you are a witness to some of the oral requests - What do you mean by that, sir - coming from the MUP? Can you be more specific? Can you direct us towards that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I mean precisely those couple of situations from the war when coordination and coordinated action between our forces and forces of the MUP were arranged, and in the course of 1998 when the actions of Siptar terrorists in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija were fought, there was also coordination, coordinated action, and cooperation, and support, of course. That's what I meant, that part. But Mr. Ivetic was quite precise. He asked me whether documents arrived from the MUP staff, supposing it was in Pristina, whether they arrived in Djakovica; such documents did not come to us directly ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look -- or focus your attention, I should say, to the paragraphs 24 through 26 of your witness statement wherein you describe, that's on the seventh and eighth pages of B/C/S and also the seventh and eighth pages of the English, where you describe your knowledge of the Operation Sekac, or chisel and P2011. First of all, if we can call up P2011, this document, once it comes up, this "zapovest," or order, first of all, am I correct that this is a command document originating from the command of the Pristina Corps, the IKM, or the forward command post, in Djakovica itself.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I made this document; its title is: "Order to crush Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Radonjic Lake."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in drafting this document, specifically section 5 of the same, which is in pages 2 through 4 of the B/C/S but pages 4 through 9 of the English. If the witness needs to review it, we could go to those pages, but I think he should know since he drafted it whether this is correct or not. Is it correct that your order contains precise assignments or tasks to smash the terrorist forces for both MUP units and VJ units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This paragraph resulted from coordination linkage and coordinated action with MUP units in Djakovica. The tasks were issued precisely. I wrote them in very precise terms because the operation chisel was very complicated. It was practically the most complex operation during the war. It was to be performed in three stages, and it was necessary for units of the Pristina Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt, but twice already -- earlier we made a distinction here between "action" and "operation." The witness keeps saying "action" and the interpretation comes through as "operation" and it's the same mistake in this document. The original is "action" and the translation is "operation." If you remember when General Lazarevic testified, he gave an explanation, and we made this distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have that in mind, Mr. Bakrac, and generally speaking it is possible to understand that the word "operation" is being used in different contexts in the English; however, we'll be particularly aware of it, as I'm sure the interpreters will, and we'll try to make that distinction in the record as we go along also. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jevtovic, with respect to this, as you said, complicated or complex tasking given to both VJ and the MUP units, am I correct that these assignments for these forces, both the VJ and the MUP, were also clearly depicted on an "odluka" map, a written map, decision.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot now recall the map. I had never seen it after that, but I emphasise what I didn't manage to finish a moment ago. The action was coordinated with MUP forces in a -- the title of paragraph 5: "Tasks of the units," we see that's it's a designation, a definition of what various participants in the action will be doing. Why was it described in such detailed terms? Precisely because the action was so complex and the intention was to avoid problems on the ground. And I know very well and I recall very well because I remember that with Colonel Kotur who signed this order went to SUP Djakovica that one time only where with the chief of Djakovica SUP and his operative officers we developed this action in coordination and we developed these details that were indispensable because it was a very complicated action, and I want to emphasise it was important primarily for our forces and our units who participated in this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question I have for you is with respect to the "odluka," map. Was there an "odluka," map, to your knowledge prepared for this action; and if so, who prepared it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I made this document, and as far as I remember -- because, really, I never saw this document after that or the map. What is written in paragraph 5 and the order itself was reflected on the map, but the map is an auxiliary document meant to orientate units in the territory and to help them find their way around better while executing tasks. But everything was stated in such great detail precisely to avoid problems in the execution of that action because it was performed from a circular basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, the question is whether there was a map, and you just say you can't remember; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot remember. I made so many maps, and all I see now is this document. I cannot recall the map, and all we used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question. Please try to confine what you're saying to answering the various questions that are put to you. It's time for us to have a break. We have to interrupt the proceedings at this stage for a short time, Mr. Jevtovic. Please go with the usher, who will show you where to wait for the next 20 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As you can see, we are without Judge Kamenova, who is unwell. She was not particularly well before we started but doesn't feel able to continue. We've considered the position and we think it is in the interests of justice to continue today in her absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, before the break we were talking about this action Sekac or chisel. In regards to that I would like to focus your attention to your written statement paragraph 26 which is in both the B/C/S and the English page 8 of the same, that's 6 -- pardon me, 5D1358, I believe -- 1385, thank you. And while we're waiting for that I can ask you the question, sir. Here you talk about the fact that Colonel Kotur and the chief of the Djakovica SUP were to be at the observation post at the Suka Vogelj feature. Now, I know you in your statement have said that there was not formal resubordination. I would like to ask you assuming for the purposes of this question that there had been resubordination of the -- of any MUP unit to the elements of the Pristina Corps at the time of this operation, wouldn't it be correct that the commander or leader -- commander of the MUP forces, the MUP superior would still have been the superior transmitting orders to his unit, that is, that the subordinated commander would still be the commander of his unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Even if it had been so, he would still have been in command of his units; however, that was not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can -- I think we're finished with Sekac and I would like to move to another area that I think you can help me with. First of all, following the conclusion of the war and specifically in the year 2001, were you posted or assigned within the office of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia during any period of time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I worked but not at the office. I worked at the cabinet --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: -- of the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. And towards that end I'd like to show you a document marked 6D1128. It's a one-page document dated the 18th of October, 2001, originating from the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia at that time and directing in paragraph 4 for a certain Lieutenant-Colonel Goran Jevtovic to -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In item 4, tasking a Goran Jevtovic to effectuate this order which effectively calls for certain originals of documents from 1998 and 1999 of the Army of Yugoslavia to be removed from the archives and to be secured in a separate location within the cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Are you familiar with this task and are you that Lieutenant-Colonel -- or at that time that Lieutenant-Colonel Goran Jevtovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this task, and I am that lieutenant-colonel in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then would you have drafted this document, 6D1128 that we see --

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in regards to your tasks effectuating this decision to remove certain documents from the archives of the VJ, I'd like to have a moment to show you something that's been used previously in this case, 6D1130, and if the cover and the first page of this exhibit can be shown to you. The question I would have for you, sir, once that document comes up is: Is 6D1130 your work product in effectuating the creation of a list for documents that were said to be removed pursuant to the order from 2001? We'll need to -- I think the first page -- if we go to the first page -- the next page, I'm sorry, page 2 in e-court, that ought to be enough for the -- and flip it, that should be sufficient for the witness to see the date and the contents and to see if this is familiar to him.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document, but I would appreciate it if learned counsel Ivetic would let me provide a short explanation. I don't know if the translation is wrong. The term that was used was "to remove." First of all, it's not -- that's what I hear in my headset, to remove. It was not about removal. It's an activity that the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, according to the Law on Archives and Records from 1998 that was in effect then and is still in effect now -- I can explain how this all came about, but that would be the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: But I do have this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to 6D1128.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was going to suggest if we could clear it up if he could have him read the first point under [B/C/S spoken] which is apparently the part where there was a translation difference between what I said in English or what was translated to the witness and what the Serbian terminology is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you, Mr. Jevtovic, if you look at item number 1, if you could perhaps read item number 1 in it entirety then we could be on the same page as to what I have been asking you about.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph states: "Make a selection and take out or separate from the archives of the Army of Yugoslavia originals of documents of the command of the Pristina Corps and the command of the 3rd Army from 1998 and 1999 and replace them with authentic and invisible [as interpreted] copies." So the word is "separate" or "take out."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't know if we need to show you again 6D1130. The question I have for you is: Is 6D1130 your work product in completing the tasks that were set forth in this order originating from the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ to separate originals and replace them with copies?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the result with the proviso that originals from the archives are not to leave army installations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say they do not leave the army installations, would I be correct that this order called for them to be secured within the cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. The reason for that -- in fact, there are a number of reasons, but the first and most important reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't need -- just answer the question. Please continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the witness wanted to explain what this document is about, and I believe he should be allowed to do that because the question was asked. In re-direct I would be spending my precious time to clarify the question asked by Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid you'll just have to do that. The question's been answered. Please continue, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually I think I'm done. I think I'm done with my questions in respect to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at your statement. I would like to ask you a couple of questions about the term you were using, "Joint Command." I would like to look at paragraph 10 of your statement, and we saw earlier in the document you were shown, Exhibit P1427, that at item 6 it was stated that the command of the operation shall be by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the forward command post in Djakovica. And in this paragraph you explain the expression "Joint Command" by saying that it referred to an operation in support of the MUP in routing terrorists. And later on you say that right before this operation MUP generals were at IKM in Djakovica in order to coordinate action and support. Do you not know of a body or a group that existed in 1998 that was referred to as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: From my superiors I heard about the term "Joint Command," and as far as I'm concerned I as an operations officer at the forward command post that was a virtual notion for me. Joint Command as an organized structure of the state, army, and MUP was not something that was present where we were at the forward command post. We did see documents, we did hear of those terms, I was familiar with that term "Joint Command." However, as for the chain of command in implementing tasks, that was in place. At the time, General Lazarevic who headed forward command post was directly subordinated to General Pavkovic, corps commander at the time. Since I'm a trained officer, I was familiar with this term, and I knew that it represented something that transpired in reality, a sort of cooperation linking coordination, support, exchange of information, and this is something that existed in our heads, in our minds. What I said to you as for the MUP generals, they did spend time there; and in that way, they agreed on how to operationalize what was done together in areas where it was done, either where we supported MUP or where certain coordination was needed given the strong forces of terrorists and the dynamics of their hostile and other attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: If I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The distinction I want to make in the question is that your definition in your statement of the term "Joint Command" and in your answer just now seem to me to refer to an activity, an activity of coordination. All I want to know is whether or not you knew of a body, a group of persons, that were referred to as the Joint Command for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know that a group of persons existed. I knew that a group of senior officers of the army and the MUP cooperated on a daily basis, exchanged information, and dealt with the then-existing problems in Kosovo and Metohija. What I was familiar with from my superior officers, I knew from them. I did not attend any meetings, I was not present at any meetings in Djakovica, nothing of that sort happened in Djakovica. The line -- the chain of command was intact, as envisaged by regulations. This is why I would like to reiterate that the term "Joint Command" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you not aware of a group including members of the MUP, including General Pavkovic, including political figures that Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, and Mr. Andjelkovic who were involved or engaged in meetings of a body referred to as the Joint Command in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the previous question of the Prosecutor. The witness responded on page 42, line 24, that he knew nothing about that. Is it really necessary to ask him ten times if he said right out at the outset that he knew nothing about it? That's what I'm wondering about, and I keep repeating that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a specific question that's being put to ensure that there's no misunderstanding, and therefore the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall the question or would you like me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I recall. Mr. Prosecutor, the group of people as you described them in your question did not exist in reality. There existed commanders of units. You are mentioning some politicians, or rather, people from the political sphere, and what I am familiar with are the representatives of the legal authorities, of the state as it existed at the time. I know that members of various parliaments came to Djakovica at the time as well as people from the political life, representatives of authorities. But as for a specific group of people in command of the units on the ground that existed as a special staff or as some special Joint Command, no, that's my answer to your question. There was a chain of command --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but you have introduced something which I didn't ask you about. I didn't get to asking you about a specific group of people in command of units on the ground that existed as a special task or as some Joint Command. I'm just asking you simply: Were you aware of those persons being involved in a group called the Joint Command? You were aware of that or you were not, were you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: -- I knew of the term "Joint Command," but as for the group and its composition, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you use the term "Joint Command," who told you to use it first?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I never used that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Because in reality --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You have disposed of that. You drafted orders including one that you were shown, P1427, in which the term "Joint Command" is used. I don't know -- I don't think we need to show you that again. And that is an -- and in your draft -- or in that order which you wrote up you said that the combat operations would be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the PrK forward command post. Who first told you or authorised you to incorporate the term "Joint Command" in orders that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In my previous answer you did not let me complete my thought, but let me tell you now, nobody had to authorise me to use it. I heard of the term for the first time, if I remember well, in early July of 1998. When I drafted several of those documents, I think that there was several of them, I as operations officer was duty-bound to copy down the heading of the document that had arrived from Pristina. So this explanation that I gave you that this term meant nothing to me, it really meant nothing to me, both in theoretical and in practical terms. I think I heard it for the first time either from Colonel Djakovic or General Pavkovic, but I can't really recall when nor was it particularly significant at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you put it in orders in the terms that I just read out, combat operations would be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the PrK forward command post in Djakovica," are you saying that this was not significant and it meant nothing in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. This term, this heading, had to be copied down because it had been awkwardly coined or used previously in Pristina. What it meant that in Djakovica at that point in time there was going to be a unified command post where there were going to be practically two structures. What it meant for our units was that if there should be a problem in terms of coordination and cooperation on the ground, they had to know clearly whom to address, whom to go to resolve a problem that they came across --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm asking you about this part of the order where you say that command operations were to be commanded by the Joint Command, and you said that it meant nothing and it was insignificant as far as you recall. But that still doesn't answer the question I asked you. Were you told about it by anyone to incorporate that term? Either you were told or you were not told to use the term "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that means that if there was a term "Joint Command" used in the heading and it was awkwardly used and General Pavkovic as corps commander signed it or General Lazarevic, that would mean that they were commanders of the Joint Command; however, we were never officially informed of that nor did they introduce themselves as such nor did I receive such information from anyone from the command nor was General Lukic a commander of such a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But -- I'm not understanding. I just want to know why you put the term here, why you put that sentence here, that combat operations are to be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. I take it from your answer that you were not told or ordered to do so. Am I understanding you correctly, that you heard this term being used informally and you decided on your own initiative to put it in the order, that combat operations should be commanded by the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't use it on my own initiative. I affirmed this with full responsibility. This term was intended for those who took part in combat operations so that they would know how to link --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, you're not answering the question. You're being asked who told you, if it was somebody who told you, to use that expression or whether you yourself decided to use it. You've said it was not your decision, so the question is: Who told you to use it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, are you referring to this specific document that the Prosecutor put to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've used it in a number of -- the expression is used in a number of documents, but you've used it in this particular one, P1427, where you've said that the operation will be commanded or the action will be commanded by the Joint Command. And the question is: What was your authority for writing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In writing documents at the lower level of command in a situation where there are documents of that nature at higher levels, there are certain rules that we have to abide by. I cannot recall now because I do not have the document in front of me, but I think that there was a document preceding this one that had come from Pristina. And this is why the heading was copied down, so this heading reads: "Joint Command," and there is the same term used in item 6. However, essentially this Joint Command represented what I have described in my statement, namely, that there is going to be a combined command post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already told us that. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that the answer satisfied you, and I think that it would be fair to the witness to put to him the document that the Prosecutor wishes him to comment on. The witness doesn't have the document in front of him, and he asked to see it in order to be able to explain it. I think it would be fair if the witness were to be shown this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do you want to see this document, Mr. Jevtovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor insists on me explaining the term, and in that case, yes, I do wish to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it will be shown to you on the screen, that's P1427. Can you tell us meanwhile where the combined command post was for this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you zoom in, please. Combined command post was at the forward command post in Djakovica. I think that it says so in item 6, or I don't know which item it is, command and communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let him see item 6, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. As it reads here: "In the premises of the forward command post in Djakovica in the then-barracks called Devet Jugovica it was there. Why there, because all communications -- there was a communications hub there. Both telephone lines and radio relay communication lines, and naturally we had many other pieces of equipment, and we had the ability to have such combined action there logistically. It was also a very significant place. We had a Heliodrom there. We had helicopters used for transport for medical purposes and that was the reason. So this is part of the order--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the abbreviated order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who from the MUP was there during the action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember certainly General Obrad Stevanovic who came for the reasons of coordination, and I think that there was also General Djordjevic there. The two of them I saw there, and the coordination unfolded as stipulated by regulations in peacetime. Nobody was in command but simply future action was harmonized, coordinated, support, coordinated action, and they raised questions concerning the implementation of tasks. Everybody implemented their own tasks and acted in accordance with what I have stated, and this is evidenced by the signature of General Pavkovic, the corps commander. And you can also see underneath where it says "forward" that our units were listed. He signed here as corps commander not as commander of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the forward command post continued to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've dealt with the question. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
