utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Jevtovic, I just wish to understand clearly on the record on what basis it is that you wrote that action was to be commanded by the Joint Command. You have told us that you didn't need to be authorised to do so, you have told us that you didn't do it on your own initiative. And in your last answer you seem to be saying, and tell me if I'm correct, that in a preceding order you saw the heading "Joint Command" used, and therefore in writing of this order on that basis because of a heading in some preceding order you decided to say that command of the action was to be by this Joint Command. Is that the reason you put "Joint Command" there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have such authorities. Something of this nature could have been ordered to me by General Pavkovic in this particular order or by Colonel Djakovic, but again on the basis of something that had been previously treated by this document. At that time I did not see any joint command or some commander of this Joint Command. Essentially, nothing changed. As for the term "Joint Command," as I have told you, I had heard of it earlier, but as far as I know, it was always used when some complex actions and operations were carried out where MUP forces and army forces, first and foremost, the Pristina Corps forces, acted together in coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it then that your final answer is that you put in this order that the action would be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija on the basis of an order from General Pavkovic or from Colonel Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be certain as to who specifically told me that, and I especially can't be certain given the passage of time. To tell you the truth, I simply don't remember, and I didn't use it on my own without authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You put it in the order in bold. Did someone tell you to do that or did you do it on your own initiative, the expression "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" on the order is in bold. On what basis did you do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The text in bold, if I'm allowed to be less formal here, is just our own artistic, creative effort. The fact that it was printed in bold had nothing to do, absolutely nothing, with the implementation of the task. The words "forward to" is also in bold. And as for this text here, coordination with MUP forces, the same goes for that as well. So my answer to you is that it has no significance that the text is in bold. It's simply an issue of mere aesthetics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is bold used in every section 6 of an order to identify the body that will command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I understood your question. In many instances in this document there is text in bold, certain headings, subheadings are in bold. The same applies here. Given that a lot of time has passed I really can't explain to you why this particular text is in bold and not some other text, just like, for example, it says here "reports" in bold and "forward" is not in bold. Essentially it makes no difference whether it's in bold or not. According to our Rules of Official Correspondence and Official Practices - and I'm quite knowledgeable of this - that has no practical meaning. This is just a mere issue of aesthetics. Nebojsa Pavkovic is also in bold; however, the word "commander" is not. I cannot remember now how come I didn't put the word "commander" in bold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the action that this order refers to, you said that General Obrad Stevanovic and General Djordjevic from the MUP side went to the premises of the command, forward command post, for the purposes, as you put it, of coordination. Who were the corresponding members of the VJ present during the action with these MUP generals?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: During the action most certainly General Pavkovic was there. I think General Lazarevic, actually I'm sure, he was not there on the day, one of the reasons being the initials here, the document was drafted by myself and Colonel Kotur. As far as I remember at the time there were incidents, serious ones along the border, even attacks I would say along the number of different axes along the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I even remember that this was in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sure what you're saying is -- might well be interesting for some reason. I just wanted to know who were the corresponding VJ member or members, and you're saying it was General Pavkovic. Would you agree with me that when army units are involved in combat operations there has to be singleness of command? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. What you asked me earlier, I never said that General Pavkovic was an equivalent of a MUP general, so there's one thing that you must bear in mind. I was only saying who was there. MUP generals and army generals especially in peacetime cannot be compared -- or in wartime for that matter, they cannot be compared because their jobs are just so different. Nor do I know any of this in theory. I'm not qualified to explain the theory behind this, but I do know there can be no comparison, especially not the type that you suggest. As for the other part of your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer the question you've been asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, Mr. Prosecutor, it was about unity of command and measures to be taken. Can you please ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you -- the question was: Would you agree with me that when army units are involved in combat operations there has to be singleness of command? And you said: "No, I wouldn't." Do you understand or have you ever in your training as an officer of the VJ encountered the term "singleness of command"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the beginning of your question. Whose operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure which question didn't you understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you asked isn't clear. The witness wants to know what combat operations you're talking about. That's a very vague and general concept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As a principle, Mr. Jevtovic, when you -- when army units are involved in combat actions or operations, isn't there singleness of command in respect to these army units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was and strict subordination, yes, that's right. I hadn't understood that. When units are carrying out combat operations there is unity of command -- singleness of command, actually, singleness of command is compulsory. It's one of the fundamental postulates of how an army works.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could answer me and tell me briefly why is it fundamental? Why is it a fundamental postulate of how an army works?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: As any army in the world, the same applied to our army, it couldn't function properly without that principle, but the same applies to NATO countries, does it not? You can't exercise command or responsibly take measures against someone if there is no clear chain of command that is responsible for all these steps that are taken. That's what our regulations say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when combat operations are being carried out you would agree with me that it is even more fundamental that there is what you refer to as a clear chain of command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly in as far as that applied to units of the Yugoslav Army, the 3rd Army, and the Pristina Corps specifically in this case. In as far as it applied to the army's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the course of the -- of combat operations or actions where, for example, General Pavkovic was present along with Generals Stevanovic from the MUP and General Djordjevic from the MUP, if there was not unanimity in respect to a decision to be taken while soldiers are engaged in combat who would have the final say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: There was no final say, simply, because there was no such resubordination or Joint Command, especially not back in 1998. The mission of an army in peacetime and in wartime is clear and the same applies to the MUP. I don't know that anybody had final say the way you put it or, indeed, that there was anybody who did as a matter of fact have final say, because our laws and bylaws and regulations are quite strict in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where there were these joint combat actions and operations with Generals Stevanovic, General Djordjevic from the MUP, General Pavkovic from the VJ present, where a decision needed to be taken in respect of a combat action or operation and there was no unanimity, is it your evidence that no decision would be taken?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It certainly would not have been taken, no decision would have been taken, or at least everybody would have gone on working independently, but it's about commitment. This is a state border that we're looking at, there were laws under which we worked under. It didn't matter whether we were enjoying any support from the MUP or not, just like they had commitments and tasks of their own elsewhere. This is how it was and this is exactly the way I understood it. When there is a mention of a Joint Command within this framework that you suggest, it didn't work this way you didn't have several army and MUP generals all sitting together in one place conferring and making decisions; I wasn't aware of anything like that going on. Actions and steps were agreed, coordinated, coordination was organized, if there was a severe problem that affected both, them and us, and whenever there were overlaps both in peacetime and wartime. It wasn't like there was someone who had final say or anyone in a position to foist anything on anyone else, at least not that I was aware of, never saw a thing like that, never heard of a thing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well then. I hear you. The operation or action on the 27th and the 28th of April in the Caragoj valley, that is what you at one point in time referred to as the Reka action; it is, correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This word, "action," as I said was used and accepted by the subordinates at the time and it was part of our jargon I would say simply because there was no specific document calling it that. The expression "Reka," meaning river in B/C/S is a matter of topography. It's something -- it's a word that everybody uses. It would have meant nothing special. We simply used this name, Reka, to conceal something, to preserve the secrecy of the action itself, otherwise it wouldn't have been called that, Reka, it would have been called "Upad," which is B/C/S for an incursion or something like that. Reka is a perfectly commonplace word used by everyone. Everybody uses it. It means "river" in B/C/S. That's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many units from the VJ were involved in that operation, do you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, as I said I was at the Morina border post at the time, and I was busy there because on those days there was a great deal happening and there were attempts at incursions all the time, but as far as I know there were about two platoons. I didn't finish answering, I'm sorry, about two platoons of the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Brigade practically turned and faced the other way in relation to the existing combat disposition in the Korenica sector. The 52nd Rocket Brigade dispatched a small company of their men from their rear battalion. I'm not talking about infantry specialists and anybody else that they had. I think about 30 men were involved from the Pristina Corps military police battalion, at least as far as I knew, and about a platoon from the 63rd Odulava [phoen] Brigade, who used to be in the Jasic village sector before that after the fighting in the Kosare sector. They were resting there and they were getting resupplies of weapons and ammunition, that sort of thing, and that's precisely what I was talking about. There were insufficient forces. There was a shortage of forces. There was a serious problem. The 137th Brigade, the terrorist brigade that we were facing, and that was our problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 63rd Brigade that you referred to is the 63rd Parachute Brigade from Nis, is it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was only a small contribution as big as a platoon. It's a very small part of that brigade, a brigade is far more large-scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm going to ask you, Witness, just to answer my question briefly. Was it resubordinated to a Pristina Corps unit; and if so, which unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure who you mean resubordinated to. Are you talking about the 63rd Brigade? Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The 63rd Brigade was resubordinated during the war to the Pristina Corps command, and the corps commander had the authority to exercise command over that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that's how it worked, it was resubordinated, but I can't think of a specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the 52nd Rocket Brigade was --

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade was from the establishment of the Pristina Corps, it was a component of the Pristina Corps used for anti-aircraft defence, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there were -- the platoons are the men from the military police battalion, who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The 52nd Military Police Battalion, it was part of the corps subordinated to the corps commander. There was this rather small unit the equivalent of a company I think comprising less men also. It was facing serious problems along the state border the losses, part of the 125th Brigade roughly at the same time and I can't be certain when exactly this smaller unit was resubordinated to the 125th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think you said that there were elements of a 2nd Motorised Battalion involved in that operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which unit were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Motorised Battalion was a battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade. As far as I remember, and I do actually remember, in the sector covered by that battalion there was the Chief of Staff of the 549th Brigade, along with the battalion commander under the establishment of course, and they were resubordinated to the command of the 549th Brigade. But they were in the immediate vicinity of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now we've got your evidence sir --

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: -- defending the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that there was no written plan in relation to this action or operation, and that is operation -- the Reka operation of the 27th and the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No plan, is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. No written plan.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No written plan, no order, no decision existed, not that I saw, plan, order, decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you find it unusual, sir, that an operation involving so many units from different brigades and some directly subordinated to the corps command would go on without a written plan, a written order, a written decision? Would you find that unusual?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It's not unusual. You say so many units or forces, this is only a very small number, this is insignificant you might say. As Mr. Bakrac was examining me I explained exactly what was going on there. As far as the army was concerned, there were some very small shifts of position, and the manpower involved was very small, exceptionally small, I should say too small, even bearing in mind what sort of an opponent you were facing in this so-called valley. A platoon is the lowest-ranking army unit in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know how many MUP units --

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- or personnel were involved in the operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what I know. I didn't go to that sector nor was I directly involved in this action. The equivalent of two companies, two companies that -- well, I don't know what their numerical strength was, but I don't think it exceeded a total of 200 men, roughly speaking. That's as much as I know, but I don't have any firm indicators. As far as I know there should have been three companies involved, but then the Pec Company for some reason dropped out and that's why there was a shortage of manpower that occurred as a result of that, and that's why they requested our assistance and that's why Colonel Kotur had to go there, to coordinate our involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at P326, and that's a map. And while it comes up, do you know where the VJ field command post was for this operation or action?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please first explain what we're looking at, what sort of a document is this? Who drew this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we get to that the question is this: Can you tell us if you know where the VJ's field command post for that action on the 27th and the 28th of April was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No. There is no command post, not even an observation post, that didn't exist. That's what I know and I know this sure and certain knowledge. I know there was no such thing. This is not an army document to the extent that I can tell, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it's not an army document for the record. This is a map that was marked by the Witness Nike Peraj. Do you know where the MUP field operation command post was during that operation or action?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, nor am I aware of that. I would have realized that they were somewhere probably, but I really don't know and I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who from the VJ side commanded the VJ units in that operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: VJ is quite a broad notion. There were the small units from the Pristina Corps that were involved, each in their own sectors, and they were -- there were commanders under the establishment that exercised commands of those units, the commanders of those units, but within their own sectors. I am certain about that. There was no command post for this action or operation. I'm talking about the operative level, the corps level, a company commander, a platoon commander with a platoon, for example, that is involved in the Korenica village sector, but I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: -- this map is reliable. Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, I have not asked you yet about the map. Please focus on my questions. You just said in answer to my question: Who from the VJ side commanded the VJ units in that operation? And you said there were small units of the Pristina Corps that were involved each in their own sectors, and they were commanders under the establishment that exercised command of these units, the command of those units but within their own sectors. Earlier you said because of the manpower issues that is why Colonel Kotur had to go there to coordinate our involvement. Where did Colonel Kotur had to go to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he didn't go because there was a problem with manpower, as you said, with all due respect; but he went there because the chief of the Djakovica SUP had called him. I don't know exactly because I wasn't there at the time, but based on the reports that I received they did coordinate their work together on this problem, but it didn't go any further than that. There was coordination and the results were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the last portion of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, where did Colonel Kotur go to to coordinate the involvement of the VJ in this operation? "Where" is a place. Where did he go to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, he went to a place where on that day the chief of the Djakovica SUP was. I don't know where exactly he was. Was he stationary on that day, was he moving about, I really don't know. I don't know where it was that he left for. The Djakovica SUP had been razed to the ground by bombs. They had to move from one place to another, it was a fluid situation, and the same applied to us. I don't know what the location was on that day. I don't know where they met. I know what he told me about that meeting and later came Zivkovic transformed this or included this in oral orders by the Chamber's leave I think a clarification is called for. I do have an example to name a specific one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, I just wanted to know what you meant when you said that Colonel Kotur went there to coordinate our involvement. Did Colonel Kotur exercise any command responsibilities over the VJ forces that were involved in that operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, definitely not, not at the time. On that day Kotur was dealing with problems at the Kosare border post, and I was dealing with problems at the Morina border post and this had nothing to do with all of this. I would still like to cite an example just to clarify for the sake of truth, for the sake of justice, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, and insofar as that is necessary you will be asked by one of the lawyers here. Just for the time being can you just focus on my questions. You are telling us now that Colonel Kotur was dealing with problems at the Kosare border post, and that is in answer to my question as to whether or not he exercised any command responsibilities with respect to the VJ units there. What you said earlier, that Colonel Kotur had to go there to coordinate our involvement. Now, when you say "our involvement," are you not referring to the VJ units that were involved in that operation on the 27th and on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, involvement is a very broad concept. We had the task to block and secure the road Decani-Djakovica and then to secure our own areas, parts of Ponosevac-Junik road and another of other obligations. That is involvement. Active or I don't know what kind of other activities are something else. It's a significant difference. You said a moment ago in Karaula -- in Kosare border post. It's not that, it's in the broader area of Kosare. Kosare had by that time had fallen, it was in enemy hands, so he couldn't have been on the Kosare border post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Witness, what I want to know is based on what you have said. I want to know who, if anybody, commanded the VJ units that were involved in this operation, and you said that Colonel Kotur was sent there to coordinate our involvement." You don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this is misrepresentation of the witness's evidence. The witness said that every commander commanded his own unit, and there was no one command post and that Colonel Kotur before the action went to talk to the MUP and organize coordination. I believe the Prosecutor should look at the transcript carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect it's that coordination that he's referring to, but perhaps you can clarify the position, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- but may I just say so before I proceed that the witness did not say what counsel just represented, and I suspect that in seeking to clarify it the witness will just adopt what counsel has said. And I think in making objections we should be careful, very careful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has already said that every commander commanded his own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, and he said the rest of what was there, has he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At one stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think you're quite right to pursue it to get clarification because it's difficult to understand how that could work. So I thought that's what you were trying --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to do, and the misunderstanding was where you referred to Colonel Kotur being sent to coordinate our involvement, and Mr. Bakrac is suggesting that gives the impression Kotur's in command of the action, when in fact his visit was to the SUP chief to arrange coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac -- very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can hear the tape, the Serbian tape, what the witness said in Serbian has that meaning, and indicates that, that he went to the MUP building for coordination, but there was no talk about when. Let the Prosecutor ask the witness when. Maybe the English interpretation suggests something different. If we hear the Serbian original it indicates this, but let the Prosecutor ask: When exactly did Colonel Kotur went to reach an agreement and perform coordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following, Mr. Bakrac. Are you saying that there is something in the Serbian that has not been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'm just saying that sometimes the meaning is difficult to get across, although we are able to understand it. I'm therefore suggesting that the Prosecutor should clarify when, when, exactly did Kotur go for that coordination meeting, when relating to the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answer's already in the answers we have because he says that following that coordination meeting Zivkovic converted what happened into orders. We know that the oral orders are said to have been given on the 26th of April, so all of that's there. Mr. Stamp, please pursue the point you are pursuing because it's of interest to us, but it looks as though you'll have to start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Colonel -- well, before I get to Colonel Kotur. As a result of this meeting that you spoke of that Colonel Kotur attended, were any orders issued by him in respect to the coordination?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Kotur did not issue any orders regarding coordination. Coordination took place before the beginning of the action. He transmitted MUP requests and the positions that had been agreed, and from what I remember, General Zivkovic issued verbal orders, in other words, implemented the results of coordination between Kotur and the chief of SUP from what he said. So it was more of a clarification what should be done by whom in that story rather than a classic planning of an action. I did not attend the meeting between Kotur and the chief of SUP, so I cannot speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that General Zivkovic issued separate oral commands to all the units that you have mentioned participated in this operation or action, including units that belonged to the 125th Brigade, units that belonged to the 549th Brigade, and units that were directly subordinated to the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: What I know now, or rather, what I can remember is that he conveyed tasks to the commander of the 52nd Battalion, or rather, the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Brigade. I believe the Chief of Staff of that brigade was present I'm sure, and to the commander of the Chief of Staff of the 52nd Brigade of anti-aircraft defence, but I cannot say that for a fact because I was physically not present during those activities. That's written, for instance, in that diary we have seen. As for the unit of the military police that was engaged there, I really don't know how they received their task. It would have been logical for them to receive it from the command of the 125th Brigade, but that is something that I neither recall nor attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, can you find a suitable place to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps we could just take it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, we have to have another break for half an hour. Could you again leave the courtroom, please, with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It you look at the map on the screen in front of you, and this is P326, Nike Peraj marked in grey the positions and the activities of the VJ and explained that the VJ blocked off the borders, so to speak, of the valley, of the Caragoj valley while VJ and MUP units pushed down the valley towards Meja and Djakovica. Would you agree with me that that's a fair assessment of the role the VJ played on that operation on the 27th and the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I could not agree, Prosecutor, but could we enlarge this picture? I could not agree. If you allow me, if Nike Peraj did this, I don't know on what basis he did it, but this picture, the lines, the grey lines that purportedly represent the army, bearing in mind the scale that I have just noticed cannot correspond to the strength or the size of the units that were engaged. According to his drawing it would seem that many more troops were engaged and whoever did this drawing cannot be consistent with reality, especially what is drawn next to the communication -- to the road Djakovica-Decani, and especially this part in the area of Korenica, Sisman Baks, Babaj Boks, and to the left towards Ilok. So this drawing at this scale, I don't know what the scale is but I'm saying this because I know the terrain, is completely unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were VJ units involved in activities in pursuing Kosovo Albanians down the valley towards Meja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Kosovo Albanians never pushed back, I never heard of any such thing. There was the very strong elite brigade of the terrorists, 137 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There must be a mistake in the translation; you're not answering the question that was put to you. Try that question again, Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were VJ units engaged in activities in pushing Kosovar Albanians down the valley towards Meja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Kosovo Albanians and terrorists are two different things to me, that's why I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were VJ units involved actively with the MUP, as indicated in this drawing in pushing as in the word you use is "terrorists" down the valley towards Meja?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago, to my mind the drawing is completely incompetent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please ignore the drawing for the moment. Listen to the question. Try to help us by answering the question, please. Now, that question is a simple one: Were VJ units involved actively with the MUP in pushing terrorists down the valley towards Meja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President. What I know is this that one unit that consisted of one part of the company of the military police, that is, around two platoons 30 to 40 men in movement protected the battle order of units that were in the first echelon, and of course acted in coordination MUP units if that's what we're going to call it; but I cannot say anything further about that because I was not on the spot and there was no -- no particular plan that would reflect this. There were contacts with terrorists according to reports received from commanders and there was pushing back in that sense, but there was also combat and some of our members were killed there, one or two from the police company, and I believe that was even an attack of the terrorists against them from what I remember and from what the commander of that temporary unit reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English translation says: "... around two platoons 30 to 40 men in movement protected the battle order of units that were in the first echelon, and ... acted in coordination with MUP units ..." Now, who were the battle order of units that were in the first echelon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first combat echelon of the Pristina Corps that was intended to defend the state border was made up of the 125th and 549th Motorised Brigade in that area. The first combat echelon in this specific case had a depth of over 5 kilometres, so there were forces at the first, most forward line of defence, and forces further behind the lines that form an echelon in combat if we look at it that way. This unit of ours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, in English this means something quite different from what you've now said. The impression in your answer is that there was a battle order of units, in other words, VJ units engaged in combat. Is that not what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not say it that way. You asked me what was the first combat echelon of the Pristina Corps, that first combat echelon performs completely different tasks on the border. The rear end of that combat echelon is exactly somewhere along the road Junik-Ponosevac-Djakovica. So that combat echelon has no direct connection with the action we are talking about here. They are defending the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why then did you say this, and I'll read more of your answer because I really don't understand it now. "What I know is this, that one unit that consisted of one part of the company of the military police, that's around two platoons 30 to 40 men in movement, protected the battle order of units that were in the first echelon and of course acted in coordination with MUP units, if that's what we're going to call it." Now, what did you mean by that and who were you referring to as the battle order of units that were in the first echelon who were being protected by two platoons of military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that the rear end of that combat echelon on the border was in significant danger from the activities of terrorists in depth in the valley of the river, or rather, the Caragoj valley. And that's what gave rise to our engagement, so the temporary unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Jevtovic, is what units of the VJ were going in the opposite direction, that's towards Meja. The question's not about who was behind at the border. So could you address that. Which VJ units were actually engaging the terrorists in the valley and forcing them down towards Meja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the temporary unit, I already explained, but it was not towards Meja. From what I know, it moved on a local road towards Ramoc village and no further. No units of ours ended up in Meja, and as far as I know that's the task that was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a unit -- distinguished Mr. President, that was in the area of Korenica village, and that's a unit from that first combat echelon that protected itself basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is what you say you've heard because you were not there to witness it; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's hard to see with the naked eye because it's a huge area, that's one thing; and second, I was not in the valley nor was I directly engaged in terms of command or any other sense. So I'm saying what I knew and from what transpired according to reports received from commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: From what you heard or read; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You wanted to say something, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't want to say anything before the witness. I believe you may have cleared this up, but I believe the misunderstanding is due to -- lies in the military term that is being used. If you want to have the witness leave the courtroom and we can try to clarify it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you -- I don't think it's necessary for that. You can clarify it if you feel it's necessary in your own re-examination. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're saying that what you know of the operations or actions and what transpired on those two days came from reports received from the commanders. These were reports that you read or heard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall now. I don't have any documents with me, but those could have been verbal reports. I don't know if there were any written reports, but it was regular reporting as in the war. There was no particular, special report about that. There was regular reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look quickly, as time is going on, at P1086. And while we are getting it, by regular reporting you mean the regular, written reports?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Regular reports in the war, not only written reports but regular reporting by telephone, radio communications, and other devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P1026 [sic] is a war diary of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade command, and if we could have a look at page 9 in the English, page 10 in the B/C/S -- sorry, page 33 in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the number of this, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 33 in the English corresponds to page 36 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see item 10 which is a last entry for the 26th of April. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: If we can zoom in a bit more because it's handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read the second sentence, if you can, of that entry.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: "From the command of the KG (forward command post) of -- we received a decision to engage units in the Reka action." The following are engaged and then I cannot make out what follows. One of the officers is engaged, but I can't see which; I can't make it out. It says -- I see here the acronym for company commander, one rifle platoon, if the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've read what you've been asked to read. Mr. Stamp, do you want him to read the whole entry or one sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Once sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's been read. Let's concentrate and try and make progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would also like you now to have a look at the second entry and that is for the 22nd of April and that's also on page 33 in the English but that is on the next page, page 37, in B/C/S. And I will just read it here. It says here that: "The 'Reka' clean-up operation began with the participation of the 1st Manoeuvre Battalion, the 1st Rifle Platoon and the 2nd Rifle Platoon of the command battalion. The Reka operation was carried out according to plan and dynamics." Now, having seen that, Mr. Jevtovic, do you still maintain that there was no plan or decision, written plan or decision, in respect to this operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: As for what you've just read out, I'm straining and I'm straining; but I just can't see it. I'm not sure which line you're referring to. I'm referring to the handwritten portion. I'm not looking at the English, I'm looking at the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was -- the page was turned. It's what the witness was trying to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you've just said, I simply can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do we have page 37 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Item 2.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I see what you have in mind. I can't read everything but I get the gist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having seen that, do you still maintain what you said earlier in answer to a question from the Bench, that --

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- the VJ were carrying out routine duties in that area and what they were doing was part of their ongoing duties in the field?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I still maintain that. May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you have.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I maintain that. This document is a document produced by a subordinate unit. As such, it says that they carried out tasks according to some plan and some dynamic, which can mean, for example, that the brigade commander perhaps produced a document of his own in that unit or maybe this term that they're using here, according to plan, was used as to who produced the document saw fit; but it's difficult for me to comment this. This is a person from a subordinate unit discussing a plan that simply didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In giving that answer are you also having regard to what you read earlier in the entry number 10 where the diary records: "We received a decision from the command group that our elements would be used in the Reka action"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, when we have documents such as this one - and I've been doing this job for years - stating: We received a decision, then it is necessary to quote the number of this decision and the filing number. That would be a professional way of recording something like that. What I see here is that the term "plan" is being used but the "p" is not capitalised. When we talk about plans in the military it's always capitalised, a capital "p," and you have a blank number, filing number, date, and so on and so forth. The way both terms, plan and decision, are used here including the term dynamic is a little random. I think this reflects the impression, the mere impression of whoever wrote this document. They don't give a number for this plan. I don't know that this plan exists if they do not quote a number or decision for that matter. There is no filing number, there is no combat code or anything like that. You saw my orders, the orders that I drafted and the numbers were always stated. This is a very colloquial use of the term plan at best, but I don't know who produced this document therefore I'm not qualified to interpret the expression plan as used in this document or the expression decision. I can state with full responsibility there was no plan, no decision, no order, and those would have been the only authoritative documents. This is a war diary, somebody kept it the way we see they did and you these expressions being used here, plan according to plan, what plan, what dated, what number. If it's a plan, it must have a code-name, mustn't it? This is a very arbitrary use of the term and we saw that with the word Reka, river, that was no code-name at all. It is a fact of geography. It was public and even people over in Albania knew about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I ask you yet again, please, to just deal with the questions you're asked. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said what you know transpired on those two days you discovered from reports, and you've said earlier that on the morning of the 27th you went to the border. Did you at any time on the day of the 27th go to the forward command post in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I spent the night between the 26th and the 27th there, I did my regular business [as interpreted] in my capacity as an operative officer, and then according to a set schedule I would go to the border itself, just as Kotur did and all the other officers. At the forward command post there would remain the security detail and maybe some signalsmen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have answered the question. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What time did you go to the border --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one thing there is an error in the transcript. It says: "I did my regular morning operative business," morning operative duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What time did you leave to go to the border on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It's been too long for me to remember exactly. I don't have any notes on that. I can speculate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Thank you. Let's move on. If you don't know, just say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know, Your Honours, it's been too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. On the 28th do you remember if you were there on the morning of that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I was. I don't know if I wasn't. I spent the night there, I suppose. I can't remember. I can't remember. It's not my intention to offend you, but I don't have any notes that could jog my memory. All I know is that I spent every single day at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not offended. I just asked because you told us in answer to a question from the Bench which was: Where were you on those days, you told us that you went to the border, so I got the impression that you were saying you were not there on the day when Nike Peraj said you were there. But you now say that probably you don't know if you were there on the 28th? In respect to Peraj, Peraj was a captain first class in the VJ. Your allegation that he made inaccurate reports which you say were documented, was he disciplined for any of these inaccurate reports that you say you documented?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "inaccurate reports," I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer the question. Was he disciplined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was reprimanded, but I can't answer that question with a simple yes or no, Your Honour. Measures were taken such as those within the remit of the security organ, several times in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we should go into private session in respect of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P1428, you spoke about it earlier in your evidence, and if you have a look at the last page you see, as we indicated, that it was signed by General Lazarevic. Do you know where General Lazarevic signed it? When I say "where," at which place was he when he signed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This is 1998 I think it was, or rather, he was in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's dated the 14th of August, 1998. Would that be the date when he signed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, that's the date of the document. Can you comment or do you know whether or not that is the date he signed it or can you answer based on the date at the front of the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I remember when this document arrived from Pristina, and to the extent that I remember, it was signed by him in Djakovica. I think that the corps commander was away because this was a time when the Chief of the General Staff was carrying out the inspection rounds with his teams in the Pristina Corps, the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: When, when did he sign it? Can you say when? If you can't, just say you can't.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Probably on that day, based on what it says. On that day. I see nothing to lead me to a different conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, your statement is 5D1385. Could you look, please, at paragraph 14 of that statement. Look about the middle of page -- of paragraph 14 you will see the following: "I think in June 1998 the state leadership adopted a decision which was endorsed by the highest military leadership that the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps could use a small part of their forces (no more than 5 to 6 per cent) to support MUP forces in preventing terrorism ..." And there's then a reference to the areas that would apply. What decision does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: What I know is that we were informed at the time that at one of the meetings of the Supreme Defence Council a decision like this had been taken, the decision that I'm talking about. And after that, what followed was an operation against the terrorists because by now this was an operation, it had turned into an operation in the sectors mentioned here. I think this was a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council or another body of a similar rank, that at least is what we were told and that is the extent to which I can comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, who told you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: One of the superiors, my superiors, it could have been Djakovic at the time it could have been Colonel Lazarevic, General Pavkovic perhaps, but I can't remember with certainty who specifically it was who said that the decision had been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by the expression "the state leadership"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: At that time it was usually the Supreme Defence Council that was implied that commanded the army, and if I remember well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what --

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: -- it was a session of the Supreme Defence Council, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What then did -- do you mean by "the highest military leadership"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the highest military leadership at that time was the minister of defence, his assistants, and of course Chief of the General Staff together with his assistants, that is, chiefs of sectors and administrations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by that they "endorsed" the decision?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I used that term here in the sense that they acknowledged the decision and the intent of the state leadership and proceeded to implement it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Had they a choice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Had they a choice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not, but I wanted to add that the minister of defence and the Chief of General Staff also participated in proposing measures. Maybe it's a clumsy term, the military leadership endorsed or supported. What I meant is acknowledged, accepted, and proceeded to implement. And generally speaking, sessions of the Supreme Defence Council were attended by the Chief of General Staff and the minister of defence. Such issues were within their purview and they were the ones who proposed measures to be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, 15, you're dealing with the expression that you've been asked a number of questions about " ... commanding being done by the Joint Command for Kosovo'" and you go on to say: " ... this clause was used for every operation of support to the MUP, and the essence is the same ..." And you've told us that the actual orders were being issued by the Pristina Corps, but the heading "Joint Command" was used. Did you mean to say that was the case every time an operation involved support by the VJ to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not always the case. This happened in one period in 1998. In 1999 that term was not even used anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that this always happened, for every operation where the VJ supported the MUP in 1998 reference would be made to command by the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not mentioned. The example of the chisel action is a case in point. That term "Joint Command" was used for a period in 1998 in a number of documents, but it was not the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're quite right. That should be redacted in fact and we should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I can finish within 15 minutes if the Chamber agrees. Maybe we can within 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're happy to continue as long as we get no howl of protests from any other quarter. None received, so please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jevtovic, we'll start from the end from the last questions asked by Mr. Stamp that's the freshest in your memory. When you say placed on stand-by, can you explain what that means.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: That means removed from his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In military terminology?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: That's the official military term, removal from duties for a grave breach of military discipline, a military infraction. All these are military terms at the proposal of the security organs of the 15th Armoured Brigade and the chief of that organ was myself. And this must be documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just explained it. Not to waste time, I don't want to show it now, but you have seen the war diary of the 52nd Rocket Artillery Brigade of anti-aircraft defence, and before I ask you my question concerning that war diary tell me, are decisions also imparted orally and is that in keeping with military rules?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's in keeping with the rules and regulations. When there is not enough time or for other good reasons, decisions can be imparted orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When a decision is imparted orally it is written in lower case and there is no number of the decision?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and that's why there is no number. In principle, that's the way it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You testified about another military term, and I believe it gave rise to a misunderstanding so I would like you to clarify it now. When you say that there was a danger to go -- of going into the battle order of units in the first combat echelon, does that mean that those units are necessarily active or are they just in position on the state border?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: They're in position at the state border, and that's their main and only task at the moment, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the area of Reka, was there a danger that the 137th Brigade of the KLA, according to the disposition might emerge behind the back of those units in the first echelon?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a clear and present danger, and that's what they did all the time, using various provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there any military unit in that Reka action that went before this one military police company from the 62nd?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there any other unit that was involved in this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm quite certain there was none, not in any sort of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you something about Mr. Ivetic's cross-examination. First of all, before we move on to Mr. Ivetic, if my understanding is correct, or rather, you tell me. You said that you had spent the night every single time at the forward command post and that after your regular morning operative business you would go straight to the state border. This was a daily routine for you, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a daily task, several nights perhaps. But throughout the war -- well, yes, but that was the duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about the 28th of April? I'll try to pin-point the date for you. On the 27th the Reka action started and it was completed on the 28th. You may try to use that as a reference point. The morning of the 28th of April were you at the forward command post in Djakovica going about your regular operative business?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the early morning and then I went to the Morina border post. The area referred to as the Morina border post, that's what I remember, because the strikes from Albania - I'm talking about the frame between the 9th of April and the 1st of May - were at their most intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic asked you about paragraph 11 of your written statement, whether you ever saw a written request by MUP for support, the assumption being that such written reports were dispatched. Where were they dispatched to, to the Djakovica forward command post or the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: They could have gone to either of these places, the forward command post of the 3rd Army or the command post of the -- or the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And where was the forward command post of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were they under any obligation to dispatch these written reports to you -- written requests to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ivetic asked you something about Operation Chisel could we please have 5D1382. Before that comes up, I will be needing page 2 of this report. The question was this: Under the assumption that the MUP was resubordinated Mr. Ivetic asked you whether the MUP commander, the MUP unit commander would still have remained in command of these units. You said yes, but that's not what happened. Could you please read for me a sentence from this combat report? You have it right there in front of you. It's the first paragraph on that page. The control of the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in English this is paragraph 3 just above item 3, focus of activities for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Be so kind as to read and comment on this sentence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: "Control of the operation. Colonel Milan Kotur with the Djakovica SUP chief at the observation post at the Suka Vogelj feature."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: This sentence, this combat report which is another one that I produced, if anything confirms everything that I've been saying about the relationship between us on the one hand and MUP on the other. It states in no uncertain terms that this is not a case of command, this is a case of control. Colonel Kotur is there on behalf of our units, is in command of our units, and the chief of the Djakovica SUP is in command of the MUP units or the PJP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. Jevtovic. Thank you. Can we now please have 6D1128. Mr. Ivetic showed you that one document about something being seized from the archives. You tried to explain -- you said you knew what that was about. So can you please now explain what this order is about. I'm giving you now a chance to explain. Can you see that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm waiting for your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Explain why this order was issued?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: It was the right of the Chief of the General Staff at the time and what about his motive, I'm basing this on what you told me. It was about taking certain documents out of the archive, the focus being on combat documents, for the purpose of producing a book on the application of the international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Stop there for a minute, please. The application of international law of war in armed conflict is P1011 in this trial. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first motive but this was the first edition of this book. There was a civilian, second, working on this, who was a journalist by professional named Ivan Markovic. It was necessary for those documents to be taken to a place where it was possible to work on them without allowing him to take them anywhere outside these military installations and facilities. The other motive was the production of this book. When I went there to collect these files from the archives, these documents, records, if you like, at this point in time they still hadn't gone as far as the archives. I found that the situation was not very conducive to the preservation of the army's archives. This was in the army museum at Kalemegdan. The archives of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army were being kept by a single guard, civilian, in the basement of the army museum. The window-panes had been shattered and these rooms were moist, humid. When I went there for the first time after that I proposed to the Chief of the General Staff for the archives to speedily be removed from that location because civilians had access there precisely because of the Law on Archives. It wasn't safe. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question is this: These files that were used for the production of this book, did that ever physically leave the premises of the army? Where was it written?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: In the premises of the Chief of the General Staff, it never left the army in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you make copies of those documents?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and these copies were consistent with the Law on Archives and then the originals were returned. This is something that the Chief of the General Staff is entitled to, as is the defence minister. There's an awkward interpretation that we often come across. The archives and all the files in it is something that a unit commander is entitled to use, especially if he was the one that he produced. There is something that is referred to as a list referring to the chain of custody of the files preserved in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just another question. My first question is: Are there any Rules of Service that envisage this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course there are. There is the Law on Archived Files of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this was adopted in 1998. And then we have rules on office work and official correspondence and amendments, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we didn't realize that this would crop up in the cross-examination. We didn't know that the issue would be raised. I have these Rules of Service here. It didn't have a number because we didn't know; therefore, I ask your permission if we could just very briefly place this on the ELMO and that's my last question. There's a particular article I would like the witness to read that from the Rules on Official Correspondence and Office Work in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I even think that this is a Prosecution exhibit, I'm not certain. I will come up with a number in case I'm right for our present purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you please read it, sir, item 13, the heading, what it pertains to, and the two articles, the two articles on taking out, of separating, material from the archives.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want item 137?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, but first read the heading to us just slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's chapter 13, item 137, the taking out of archived material from an archive institution. Item 137 reads: "Archive material may be taken out from the archive institution of the command for temporary use. This taking out is conducted on the basis of a request of -- for archive material form KN7," and then this is elaborated further in the following items or paragraphs. What is important here is as follows. Archive material, regardless of when it was created, whether it was at peacetime or in wartime, as a rule needs to be preserved for three years within a unit, at least three years. Certain documents need to be kept for longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We are not interested in the rest of it. You have answered my question, and my final question is: Everything concerning the taking out of this material based on this order for the purposes of writing this book was everything done in accordance with the Rule on Legislation, rather, regulations of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This was kept in the office of the Chief of the General Staff, and when the then-chief left the position, there are many witnesses that can give evidence about how this book was produced and how the archive material was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Exhibit P1548, the Rules on Office Procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what the witness read out. That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevtovic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume here tomorrow at 2.15.
